item.title: Implementing the Applied Cryptography Course Projects
item.author: raphaeltannous@proton.me (Raphael Tannous)
item.description:
You should be familiar with the drand network and check what I’ve built at appliedcryptography.me before reading this post.

The drand group provides typescript and go clients to fetch and verify the fetched rounds from the network and I wanted to create frontends for each network mode they provide, mainly: default and quicknet.

I was limited to only Rust or Go to do these projects, and since I am a Go developer, I chose Go.

The drand group provides github.com/drand/go-clients as a library to fetch and verify randomness and it works great. However, using it made the WASM file around 30MB, and that is a lot for a simple page, so I needed to find another solution. The reason why the WASM file size was around 30MB is because the drand’s go client (check go.mod) depends on the entire universe.

I started writing goLOTO and created a custom client that only depends on the cryptographic libraries provided by drand, github.com/drand/kyber. The WASM file size dropped to around 12MB. I was okay with that file size since I am hosting the frontend using Cloudflare Pages. But I kept searching to see If I can minimize the file size.

I knew that I can use tinygo to build the WASM file. However, I wasn’t able to fetch using net/http because it is not yet supported (github issues), but the app was build and the WASM file dropped to around 5MB.

I finished writing goLOTO and started writing goTimeLock. I needed to create a client for the quicknet network and the code was pretty much the same as the goLOTO code, so I created a minimal client for the drand network, codeberg.org/raphaeltannous/drand, and I was able to build around it any frontend that I want with minimal dependencies.

Using Go’s internal folder structure. I built 3 goTimeLock projects that share the same internal code:

  1. Command-line utility.
  2. Web application.
  3. Automatic decryption server.

I wanted the goTimeLock to be compatible with github.com/drand/tlock so I used github.com/filoSottile/age for hybrid encryption and made every ciphertext created by tlock or goTimeLock to be decryptable by either.

I’ve written these projects without using AI and learned a lot of things throughout the way (You can too!).

Until next time. Good bye :)

item.title: You Don't Need a Build System
item.author: raphaeltannous@proton.me (Raphael Tannous)
item.description:
I’ve deployed my website and the digital garden to Cloudflare pages and things are going great. However, the CI/CD pipeline was a mess until I settled on a simple system that just works.

At first, I tried to use Github Actions to build the Hugo site and deploy it, but it had its quirks. Then, I tried to used Cloudflare’s automatic build system, but it was messy.

I asked myself: “Why do we need a remote build system for a frontend site?”

I am already building the Hugo site locally, to review the changes that I am making. Why do I need to wait minutes for Github Actions or Cloudflare to create a container, set up the environment, and build the site?

The public directory already contains the files that need to be published, so I had an idea to create a repository in it, but can I?

YES!

If you are building a Hugo site, and have a .gitignore file, you’ve probably have public in it. The question now is, can I create a repository inside another repository, if that repository ignores the repository that I am about to create?

YES!

The build system is now simple:

  1. Build the Hugo site locally.
  2. Change directory to public.
  3. Push changes.

Now Cloudflare will just have to clone the repo and publish it (it takes seconds).

Keep your pipeline simple :)

Bye-Bye!

item.title: Completed "Build Your Own Shell" Challenge
item.author: raphaeltannous@proton.me (Raphael Tannous)
item.description:
I completed the Codecrafters’ “Build Your Own Shell” challenge in Go using only the standard library. Codecrafters is a decent platform for learning by building real-world projects, and I was comfortable using the tooling they provide.

The challenge was easy to follow, it felt like solving sequential LeetCode problems from start to finish, and there was no hidden edge cases or any vague descriptions. However, in part Builtin completion #QP2, they suggested to use a third party library for readline which is chzyer/readline. chzyer/readline has zsh-style completion, where you can Tab to choose between the suggestions, not like bash-style where the suggestions are printed to stdout. This was misleading, because the challenge build a bash-like shell, not zsh, and I spent time removing zsh features from chzyer/readline.

I dropped chzyer/readline and did not look for any third party libraries that implement bash-like readline. I restarted the challenge and built everything using the standard library, and that’s when I learned the most. An implementation of readline will abstract the learning process. You will learn the library, not how it works under the hood.

I’ve implemented everything using the standard library, and I learned a couple of cool things about terminals:

  • The terminal can be in raw or cooked mode, and for the shell we wanted the terminal to be in raw mode.
  • Escape sequence for actions like the up arrow, where it sends the bytes \x1b[A.

The hardest part was implementing pipe redirection and background jobs. I faced a deadlock :) implementing pipe redirection, and that’s because I forgot to clear the stdin when piping, and the goroutine kept hold of it, which resulted in a deadlock.

It was fun building GoSH, and I was happy building it using Codecrafters, because it gave me confidence that my code was right and showed me that test-driven development is important.

If you want to do the challenge, I suggest building it without using any third party libraries to get the most out of it, and please do not use AI.

The code for goSH can be found at codeberg.org/raphaeltannous/goSH under the MIT license.

Happy Goding!

item.title: Migrated to Codeberg
item.author: raphaeltannous@proton.me (Raphael Tannous)
item.description:
The main reason that I am leaving github is that I was not recieving emails correctly. I updated my email address, but I was still receiving emails at my old email address.

When I started migrating, I noticed that mpv-copyStuff had issues and pull requests that I did not know about. They were not in the main home page, nor in the notificaiton section.

Migrating was smooth. I just used the tool provided by codeberg. However, I had a little problem migrating my website1.

After a couple of weeks on codeberg. I really like it. The platform just works for me, and the UI is minimal.

  1. I fixed that problem by using codeberg for the hugo source code and github for the public directory, because I cannot connect cloudflare pages to codeberg. ↩︎
